name: Park Flower Beds and Mowing (rating + ranking)
description: Faithful replication of the online photo survey in Corinne Gwen Muir (2021), "Biodiversity and amenity in urban parks and greenspaces", PhD thesis, University of Warwick, Chapter 5 and Appendix 3.6. The survey has 42 photographs that the author took in Coventry parks. They show three types of floral display, perennial bedding, seasonal bedding and Pictorial Meadows, either early in the season or in full bloom. They also show three mowing styles: long, short and striped grass. In 7 questions participants rate three photos each from "Dislike a lot" to "Like a lot", and in 7 questions they rank three photos from 1 to 3. The 14 photo questions, and the photos within each question, appear in random order. Participants then say what they liked and disliked, whether wildlife value or cost would change their choice, and how they feel about park management (7 statements). The survey ends with park use and questions about the respondent. In the thesis, 407 people responded online in 2018–19, 244 of them completely. Perennial bedding was liked most early in the season and Pictorial Meadows in full bloom; seasonal bedding came last, and long grass was the most liked mowing style. The page stores the per-photo means from Appendix 3.3. The photos and questions are from the thesis (CC BY 4.0), used as published with credit to the author. This template will be removed if the author objects. Differences from the original study: (1) it runs on SP-Survey instead of Qualtrics; the photos are shown at the thesis's 300-px width, without click-to-enlarge; (2) ranking is done by tapping photos in order instead of with 1/2/3 drop-downs, and a ranking must be completed or left empty; (3) the bedding type of each photo comes from the thesis's Appendix 3.3. For Q9 the appendix repeats the Q10 Pictorial Meadow thumbnail, so the Q9 Pictorial Meadow photo was identified as the remaining photo of that question. The mowing types were read from the photos and agree with the thesis's results text; (4) the welcome text leaves out the contact details; (5) as in the appendix, the Likert scale runs from "Like a lot" in Q2, Q4, Q6 and Q8 and from "Dislike a lot" in Q3, Q5 and Q7; the order of the answer options is not randomised.
author: Muir, Corinne Gwen
